do differently because some of these mistakes cost me shots that I just can't get back. It's
not like you can just magically transport yourself back to your trip and do the shot again. So,
I'm going to tell you what I would do differently so that you don't [music] make the same mistakes.
For those of you who are new to my channel, my name is Jordan Hetrick. I'm the best selling
author of books about how to use the X5, and I've also got this YouTube channel where I give
you guys lots of helpful tips. The Insta 360 X5 is one of my favorite [music] cameras to travel
with because it's so versatile. I've taken it all over the world with me. So, let me share
some of my X5 travel tips that you don't want to miss. The first thing I would do is just pack my
mounts as if they're as important as the camera itself. Because in a lot of these countries,
you're not going to be able to buy your Insta360 accessories or any way to mount your camera. So,
next trip, I'll definitely think about exactly what shots I'm looking for on this trip. Think
about what pole you want. If you need accessories for filming in the water or mounting to a vehicle,
you just want to make sure you pack all those before you go. The second thing I would definitely
do is check with the airline and see what the restrictions are for invisible selfie sticks. If
you're just traveling with carry-on bags, some of the airlines like Ryan Air in Europe, for example,
won't allow invisible selfie sticks in your backpack. So, you want to make sure you pack those
in a check-in bag and don't get to that security line and all of a sudden be scrambling trying not
to miss your flight and trying to get this pole into a check-in bag cuz that happened to me. I'm
not going to do it again. The third thing that I will always do before I go on a trip [music] is
make sure I have a spare replacement lens for my X5. If that lens gets scratched, sand can scratch
it. You can drop it. You never know what's going to happen. If you have a replacement lens, it's
super easy. Just swap it out and you can keep on filming. And most likely, wherever you're going,
you're probably not going to be able to find one of these replacement lenses on hand in a store.
So, get one now and make sure you pack it in your bag before you go. The next thing I'm going
to do differently is to set those anti- flicker settings appropriately for whatever country I'm
going to. You might not want to set them before you go get on the plane in case you're filming on
the way to your trip. But as soon as you land in that country, make sure that your anti- flicker
settings match the [music] country you're in. It's really easy to find out which countries use 50 or
60 Hz lighting systems. And then when you're there, you'll just nail those night shots and
get them perfect. Having those settings correctly is going to prevent flickering lights when you're
filming at night. And the X5 does some great night shots using that pure video mode. So,
you just want to make sure that your camera is set properly to avoid ruining that footage. You don't
have to think about it when you're just trying to have a good vacation. [music] On my next trip,
I'm definitely going to film more and not less. You might as well film as much as you can capture
those scenes and sites, and you can delete them later, but you can't go back and refilm those
shots if you didn't film it when you were there. Sometimes I think I captured it all,
but then when I go to replay the videos and start to make a little edit, I realize, man,
I didn't get that shot I wanted. I should have just filmed it when I was there because there's no
really going back and doing it over. Another thing I do differently is capture that magic shot when I
think of it. If I'm walking around somewhere and I see something that I think would be a great shot,
it's really easy to just walk past it and continue on your trip, take a second, stop,
and film that shot because that's going to add to your whole memories, your collection of memories
and all the footage that you get. Stop, pause, get the shot, and then carry on. And then you'll have
some great footage at the end of your trip. Which leads me to the next thing that I'm definitely
going to do, and that's edit it as I go. Even if it's just a little bit. I feel like with 360,
a lot of times you're filming and you have a certain vision for what you're filming.
But because you're recording that full 360 sphere, when you go back to edit it a month later,
you might not remember exactly what you're trying to capture. So if you do have some of
those special shots that you filmed and you're like, "Oh, I captured the magic. I just want to
portray that and show what I was trying to film." Do a little edit on that clip that night. Just
go to your hotel room or wherever you're staying. Make a little edit. It's going to be one of those
memories that you create that you can actually match what you're trying to film. So I think
it's really important to at least get those key shots and then you can edit the rest later. you'll
have a lot to work with cuz you filmed a lot based on my last tip I just told you. Also, you should
subscribe to my channel so if you're out there traveling and I come out with some new videos,
you'll be the first to know about them and it might be just the inspiration you need. Next time,
I'd definitely also download footage more often. You're going to record a lot of great footage and
you don't want it all stored on this little micro SD card in your camera. If you lose the camera,
the footage is gone. But if you've downloaded it and you lose your camera, well, you're out
of camera, but you're not out the memories. And the single biggest mistake that I made in my
last trip that I don't want you guys to make is to accidentally delete files that you want to keep.
If you're going fast, it's pretty easy to tap on the screen and accidentally select all the files
instead of just a few selected files. I was just going way too fast and I accidentally selected all

no." So, I powered the camera off and I saved a few of them. But, I did lose some of my favorite
memories from the trip. So, that is a big no no. really slow down and make sure you're deleting
only the files you want to delete. And the last thing that I'm definitely going to do on my next
trip that I've done every time before is to make sure to have a good time because when you're out

clips.title: Insta360 X6 vs X5 vs DJI Osmo 360: THIS is the BEST 360 Camera!
comment_snippets: The X6 is a great camera! What do you think of the X6? There's a limited number of Creator Gift Packs available. If you'd like to take advantage of this offer, use the following link: https://bit.ly/X6_MountMedia
Waiting for Osmo 360 | |
Thanks for the very detailed review!

caption_lines.text: The Insta360 X6 is here. And this clip was created automatically by the camera and the app.
No reframing, no editing – Zero Edit – one of the X6’s particular strengths. And the result is good,
significantly better than with previous tools. The X6 features three different automated editing
functions. I’ll show you how they work a little later. But apart from that, what else is new with
the X6, and just how good is the camera really? To find out, I compared the X6 to the best 360
cameras currently available. The X5 and the DJI Osmo360. The Osmo360 2 is due to be released soon,
but only in China. There is no information yet regarding an international release, and
a launch in the US is unlikely – the X5 and the Osmo360 are therefore currently the best cameras
for comparison.There are 10 categories that are important for the quality of a 360 camera. Take
a close look at all the categories, because there are a few interesting surprises. At the end, I’ll
tell you whether I think an upgrade makes sense and what special offers are currently available.
The X6 was provided to me by Insta360 for testing purposes, but this video does not
include any additional paid sponsorship! For the first time in a long while, Insta360
has completely redesigned the body of its 360 camera with the X6. The X6 no longer has that very
elongated shape. It’s slightly wider than the X5, but significantly shorter. In terms of form alone,
it’s a compromise between the X5 and the Osmo360. It still works well with a selfie stick, and the
slightly shorter form factor is better suited for mounting on a helmet or chest mount. In terms of
volume, it’s about the same size as the Osmo360 and slightly smaller than the X5. At 195 grams,
it weighs slightly more than the Osmo360 and just a bit less than the X5. Especially when
compared to the Osmo360, the X6 has a few key advantages. It features a significantly larger,
high-quality OLED-display. The X5’s display is similar in size, but its vertical format makes
it less suitable for single-lens shots. To make room for the X6’s large OLED display, the physical
buttons were moved to the side. In their place, two virtual buttons were added at the bottom
edge. Similar to modern smartphones, they provide haptic feedback when pressed. If needed, you can
even turn the entire screen into a record button. The display and camera feel very high-quality,
and the virtual buttons work very well—so well, in fact, that I hardly ever used the physical buttons
during my test recordings. Of course, that will be different in the winter when wearing gloves. And,
of course, the lens can be replaced on your own. Similar to the X5, there’s a Lens Replacement Kit
that lets you replace a damaged lens on your own. And that’s important: even though Insta360 says
the lenses have been reinforced and are supposed to be significantly less prone to scratches,
the protruding lenses are still a weak point of a 360 camera, since they can be easily damaged.
What I also like is that replacing a lens is now much easier than on the X5. And the lenses are
certainly one of the Osmo360’s biggest weaknesses in this comparison. On the one hand, you can’t
replace them yourself; you have to send the camera in if they’re damaged. On the other hand, the Osmo
360’s lenses can fog up, for example when there are extreme temperature differences, such as when
used in water. I also ran a similar test with the X6, and unlike the Osmo 360, it doesn’t fog up.
Incidentally, the X6 is waterproof to a depth of up to 20 metres without an additional dive case.
That’s more than the X5 or the Osmo360, which is only waterproof to a depth of 10 metres.
It all looks good—smaller, very well-built, a high-quality display. But ultimately,
what matters most is the image quality and how the footage looks.
Whenever a new camera is released, there’s always discussion about sponsored reviews. For me,
the solution is quite simple: I’ll explain the key differences to you and show you several
longer comparison clips that are unedited except for reframing. This way, you’ll be
able to form your own independent opinion. The X6 features two all-new 1/1.1-inch
sensors and improved chips. The new sensors are completely new square Sony sensors,
designed specifically for Insta360. At 1/1.1 inches, the new sensors are the
same size as those in the Osmo360 and larger than the X5’s sensors, which measure 1/1.28 inches.
When we compare the footage from the X6 with that from the X5, only minor differences are noticeable
at first glance. Both clips were reframed using the Field of View Mega. Interestingly,
the X5’s field of view is slightly wider. But there are a few other interesting differences.
The colors differ slightly. Especially here in the shots of this mountain meadow, the
X6’s colors appear more natural—they more closely match reality—the meadow is greener in reality,
just as it appears on the X6, and does not have the orange tones of the X5. Here’s a comparison
shot I took with an iPhone. But that’s perhaps the most noticeable difference in the colors. Much
greater and more significant are the differences in dynamic range. Compared to the X5, the X6 has a
clearly improved dynamic range, and highlights are preserved much better. You can see that,
for example, here in the background with the sun. And even more so in this shot here in the office.
You can clearly see how the details in the window are more blown out on the X5. Or in this example
with the castle. And there’s something else that stands out here. In some cases, the X5
shows unsightly blue lens flares. That’s not the case with the X6. In my opinion, the X6 comes
with very high-quality lenses, and I’ve actually never noticed any unsightly lens flares, even when
shooting against the sun. For me personally, this is one of the most important improvements in image
quality on the X6. By the way, there are no longer any settings for Adaptive Tone or HDR on the X6.
I see hardly any differences when it comes to detail—here’s a comparison at 400%. Both shots
show a similar level of detail. How does it compare to the Osmo360? Compared to the X5,
the Osmo360 produces shots with slightly less saturation. For these comparison shots,
I also used the standard field of view on both cameras. And these comparison shots don’t look all
that different either. It’s interesting that the Osmo360 often uses more magenta tones than the X6.
That wasn’t always the case in comparisons between DJI and Insta360 cameras. You can also see that in
this shot of the meadow on the mountain. The X6’s shot renders the meadow significantly greener than
the Osmo360’s. Sometimes, when shooting against the light, the Osmo360 tends to underexpose the
shot slightly. This makes the subject appear somewhat underexposed, as in this shot here. But
overall, both cameras take very good shots. The Osmo360’s dynamic range is better than that of the
X5 and very similar to that of the X6. There are only very minor differences. In this shot taken
here in the office, the X6 performs only slightly better. The black T-shirt shows slightly more
detail in the X6’s shot, and the highlights are also preserved slightly better. Similar to the X5,
the Osmo360 can also have issues with lens flares in certain situations—and in this comparison,
you can see that the X6 handles lens flares significantly better than the Osmo360.
There’s one important topic we haven’t even touched on yet: Just like the Osmo360, the X6
can shoot in 8K at up to 50 frames per second. The X5 offers a maximum frame rate of 30 frames per
second in 8K. This is a significant upgrade, especially for those who prefer a slightly
smoother, more natural look. On the other hand, I’m a bit disappointed with the 360 slow-motion
footage. The X6 shoots in 4K at up to 100 frames per second, just like the Osmo360. The X5 is the
only one of the three cameras capable of shooting in 4K at 120 frames per second. On top of that,
I find that the X6’s image quality in 4K100 isn’t optimal, and that the X5, in particular, produces
better slow-motion footage in 4K. We’ll see that, fortunately, when it comes to slow motion, the X6
has a significant advantage in Single Lens mode. And the X6 has another feature that’s been long
overdue for Insta360. It supports 10-bit Log recording, even in 8K. The X5 does have a LOG
color profile, but only in 8-bit. Furthermore, the X5’s LOG profile isn’t available in 8K—only
in 5.7K. The Osmo360, on the other hand, also features a 10-bit Log profile that lets you
shoot in 8K. However, this is D-LOG M, and as you can see here, D-LOG M is nowhere near as flat as
the X6’s new Log profile. As a result, the dynamic range of the X6’s Log profile is better than that
of D-LOG M on the Osmo360. I converted these two clips using the manufacturers’ LUTs, and
unlike the Osmo360, the X6 produces a very neutral image that’s well-suited for further processing.
But the X6 has another important advantage when it comes to color profiles. It’s the first 360 camera
capable of capturing 8K 360 footage in 10-bit HDR Dolby Vision. This means footage where,
in particular, the highlights can be displayed much brighter. To take advantage of this, however,
you’ll need an HDR-capable display, such as the screen of a modern smartphone or a modern TV. As
you can see here in this direct comparison, the HDR footage has significantly more contrast and
looks more realistic. As my YouTube review isn’t an HDR video, I can’t show the full
dynamic range. But I get the impression that HDR videos sometimes look a bit overexposed,
even when viewed on a smartphone. Insta360 could do with making some improvements in this area.
You can reframe your 360 Dolby Vision video as usual and export it as an HDR Dolby Vision video.
This is a great feature for anyone who frequently watches their videos on a smartphone or TV.
The X6 has also made slight improvements in low-light performance. The X6 is the
best 360 camera to date for shooting in low light. Similar to the X5 and the Osmo 360,
it has its own dedicated shooting mode for use in low light. However,
the difference compared to the X5 isn’t that big. Especially considering the size of its sensor,
the X5 already takes very good shots in low light. It’s also extremely dark here. Actually,
you shouldn’t really be filming in such lighting conditions. But this scenario is
simply better suited for comparison shots and to better highlight the differences. As I said,
the difference compared to the X5’s footage really isn’t that big. The X6’s footage has slightly less
image noise and is a bit sharper. And here, too, you can see that the issues with lens flares have
been resolved. The same applies when compared to the Osmo360. The Osmo360’s footage is darker and
lacks some detail. As mentioned at the beginning, the Osmo360 has sensors the same size as the X6.
This means that the performance of the Pure Video mode is simply the deciding factor,
as was also evident from the X5’s good results. But you can’t say that the X6’s lead is huge.
Interestingly, the differences in Single Lens mode are perhaps greater overall than in 360
mode. The X6 clearly performs better here. This is true both when compared to the Osmo360 and
when compared to the X5. The colors in the X6’s recordings look better, and they also show more
detail. And that brings us to a topic where the X6 has made great progress: the single-lens mode.
As we’ve just seen, the X6 clearly performs best in low-light conditions among all three cameras
in Single Lens mode. But that’s not the only improvement Insta360 has made in Single Lens
mode. All three cameras can capture flat footage with just one lens, which you no longer need to
reframe. And just like the Osmo360, the X6 can now also capture flat footage in 5K at up to 60 frames
per second. On the X5, the maximum is 4K60. As you can see here on the camera, with the X6 you can
set the field of view relatively freely in Single Lens mode and also enable distortion correction.
That’s really cool – the footage in Single Lens mode looks good, but I’ve also noticed that the
Osmo 360 and the X5 apply more HDR processing. The highlights can blow out a bit more quickly
on the X6 in Single Lens mode. I don’t know if that might change with a future firmware update.
what I’m really excited about is that with the X6 in Single Lens mode, you can now also shoot
slow-motion footage in 4K at up to 120 frames per second. This is also possible with the Osmo 360,
but only in the extremely wide ‘Boost’ mode. With the X6, 4K120 is available in Single
Lens mode regardless of the field of view. This means the X6 is increasingly capable of
replacing a traditional action camera. High-quality slow-motion footage has
been one of the few remaining exclusive features of a standard action camera.
Of course, all three cameras still have several other shooting modes, such as for time-lapses
or hyperlapses. Just like the Osmo360, the X6 can take 360 photos with up to 120 megapixels.
I’ve done a comparison of a few photos here in the office, as many people are interested in
indoor 360° photos. This is a heavily cropped version of the photos. Unlike the Osmo360,
the X6 has a significantly higher dynamic range, also because it features an HDR mode. The level
of detail is also slightly better than on the Osmo360. Compared to the X5, there’s a
noticeable improvement in detail, partly because the X5’s photo has significantly fewer megapixels.
There have also been improvements to the Bullet Time mode. The Bullet Time mode is
now available for the first time in 8K at up to 100 frames per second. But I find
the Instaframe mode—which is exclusive to the X6 and X5—much more interesting. In Instaframe mode,
you can select a subject and track it directly in the camera, much like you would with a gimbal
camera. You’ll then get a perfectly reframed flat clip in 4K with the “Invisible Selfie
Stick” effect. No more editing required. The tracking and reframing are therefore performed
directly in the camera. If needed, you can also simultaneously record a 360 backup clip in 8K,
which you can reframe yourself—just in case you’re not satisfied with the flat clip.
Simultaneous recording in 4K and 8K—that’s not possible with the X5. When recording a
flat clip and a 360 clip at the same time, the resolution on the X5 must be reduced to 1080.
And that brings us to a topic that sets the X6 and Insta360 apart. The goal is to increasingly
relieve users of the need to edit and reframe their footage. After all, reframing is still
considered the biggest drawback of a 360 camera. To take the reframing off the user’s hands, the X6
supports a new, completely revamped Autoedit feature in the app. You select a few clips,
and the app does the rest. Until now, the results were rather average. That has now actually been
improved. By the way, the intro clip was created using the new Auto Edit feature.
But there are two more new features. With the new AI Director feature,
the X6 analyzes all clips recorded that day at the end of the day and while charging,
identifies highlights, and automatically transfers a custom-generated daily vlog to
your smartphone—all fully automatically—you don’t actually have to do anything except activate the
feature. Everything runs on the camera and app. No upload to the cloud is required for this feature.
With AI Director, you don’t even have to select the clips yourself. This feature automatically
compiles a montage of some of the best shots of the day, which you can share straight away.
In contrast, the new cloud features, Moments & Moments Pro, which work in conjunction with Google
Gemini, are quite different. After you’ve uploaded your clips to the cloud, Moments Pro becomes a
kind of personal editor. The clips are analyzed, and various editing schemes are suggested. You
can then select different tags or protagonists and start the edit. This process takes place entirely
in the cloud, and you’ll be notified as soon as the video is ready. The feature is interesting and
works well, but there’s a catch—you’ll naturally need a cloud subscription to take advantage of it.
depending on the keyword, it can also pick out key scenes from older,
perhaps even forgotten, recordings. All three features represent an upgrade
to the previous AutoEdit function. Generally speaking, in my opinion, it’s not about getting
the best possible result from your footage. Rather, it’s about getting a good montage of
your footage quickly and easily, without having to do the editing yourself if you don’t feel
like it. And the results can be really cool! But that isn’t a feature exclusive to the X6.
all the new automated editing features will also be available for the X5. If you’d like to find
out more about the new Autoedit features, have a look at my tutorial on the subject.
I’ll include a link to it in the description. With all these new features and the smaller
form factor, the question of recording time naturally arises. So how long can the X6 shoot,
and are there any overheating issues? I ran a test here in the office at 8K30 at
a warm 26 degrees Celsius and without any airflow. Under these unfavorable conditions, there were no
overheating issues whatsoever, and the X6 was able to shoot for an incredible 2 hours and 38 minutes.
That’s 1 hour and 10 minutes longer than the Osmo360 and the X5. Only the X5 had overheating
issues under these conditions and shut down after 56 minutes due to overheating. Of course,
it’s worth noting that in real-world use and with airflow, none of the three cameras will have
overheating problems. For most people, overheating will therefore remain more of a theoretical issue.
But Insta360 has gotten everything right this time when it comes to overheating and battery life.
To capture shots like this one or this underwater shot, a 360 camera requires
very specific accessories. And in this regard, not only the X6 but also the X5 have a major—if
not decisive—advantage. It’s true that all sticks and mounts are compatible with all 360
cameras. But Insta360 is the only manufacturer so far to offer an Invisible Dive case for its
360 cameras. And only with such a dive case can you take 360° shots underwater, since underwater
shots place entirely different demands on lens stitching. Unfortunately, the Dive Case for
the X6 wasn’t available at the time of my test, which is why you’re seeing footage from the X5
here. But a Dive Case for the X6 will be available soon. However, a dive case is now also available
for the X6. Apart from that, there are several remote controls, ND filters and other special
mounts and accessories available for the X6. And have you seen this: the Luna Ultra’s POV
Head Tracker? It’s worn like a headset and is also compatible with the X6. When using the
Instframe mode, The framing automatically adjusts to the movements of your head.
Personally, I wouldn't want to do without the DiveCase. For me personally,
the lack of an Invisible Dive Case is one of the Osmo360’s major weaknesses
I know that many users aren't particularly interested in audio quality. But Insta360 has been
constantly working to further improve the audio quality of its cameras—and the X6 is no exception.
The X6 features a new Windproof 360 microphone. The camera has microphone openings on all sides
that are protected from the wind. And of course, the X6 also includes the excellent
Voice Enhancement mode, which effectively filters out background noise. But of course,
for even better audio quality, there are external microphones available for all
three cameras. The best choice for the X6 is definitely the relatively new Mic Pro.
What else is important? What other differences are there between the three cameras? The X6 also
comes with a very special feature: 3D Spatial Capture. Put simply, this is a technique that
creates a 3D model from a video or photo – a 3D model within which you can move around freely.
This is a particularly important upgrade for anyone who uses their 360° camera professionally,
for example for virtual tours. You don’t just get a photo where you can look around freely;
you get a high-quality 3D model in which you can move around freely. For example,
a house that you can explore virtually and freely. For many people, this is certainly a very cool
feature. Unfortunately, 3D Spatial Capture is not available in the US at launch for technical
reasons. However, this is set to change. And for me, very important:
Unlike the X5, the X6 finally has internal storage. At 47 gigabytes, it’s only about
half as much as the Osmo 360, but it’s enough in case you forget your SD card. And, of course,
the apps are important, too. Especially when compared to other manufacturers, the Insta360 apps
are still the best in terms of feature set. This applies to both the smartphone app and the desktop
app. That said, you can of course also reframe your clips quite well with the DJI Mimo app.
I think the X6 has turned out to be a fantastic camera that gets almost everything right. And
the new AutoEdit features and 3D Spatial Capture expand the functionality of a 360-degree camera.
Of course, that comes at a price. The Insta360 X6 starts at $699 in the U.S. and at €699 in Europe.
That’s the only real downside of the X6 in this comparison, since the X5 is already available
starting at $550 or €590 in Europe. The Osmo360 is similarly priced, but you can find it cheaper from
third-party retailers like Amazon. You’ll find links to all three cameras in the description
below. If you use the link for the X6, You'll also receive an exclusive creator gift pack. It's
supposed to be an extremely useful Double Lens KIT that lets you replace two damaged lenses.
So check out the offer—it's a limited-time deal, so you'll want to act fast if you're interested.
If you have an older camera, there’s also a trade-in program you can take advantage of. This
applies to DJI and GoPro cameras as well. I’ll include a link to this in the description too.
So what would I recommend? In my opinion, the X6 has turned out to be a perfect 360 camera. It has
hardly any flaws, and aside from slow-motion in 360 mode, there’s hardly anything more you could
ask for right now. I really like the new lenses and the fact that all the lens flare issues have
been fixed. The new automated editing options are cool, too. It’s basically a flawless camera,
though it doesn’t have any absolutely standout killer features. If you’re buying a new camera
and can afford it, I’d go with the X6. But if you want to save some money, the X5 and the Osmo360
are still very good alternatives. Give me a like as feedback if you found this video interesting.
A detailed beginner’s tutorial on the X6 will follow soon. So stay tuned, and see you next time.

caption_lines.text: ﻿If you're getting ready for your next big travel adventure
and want to capture cool and unique shots
on your journey without missing anything,
then 360 cameras really are the perfect choice
for their versatility and ease of use.
To make a great travel video however, you're going to need to make
some important shooting and editing decisions that can ultimately make or break your video.
So, in this video, I'll guide you through the five most
important steps you'll need to follow in order to
make a great travel vlog with your 360 camera.
Step One is choosing the right camera gear
to bring with you on your travels, and that obviously starts with your 360 camera.
Right now, I'm using the Insta360 X3;
however, there are many other great cameras out there,
and no doubt plenty more to come in the future.
The next must-have accessory is an SD card,
and if you're travelling, you're likely to be shooting a lot of clips, which is why
I'd recommend one with a high memory capacity so you can capture as many clips as you like
without ever having to worry about running out of space.
At an absolute minimum, I'd recommend
this 256 gigabyte SD card from SanDisk. On the high end, you can go for the full one-terabyte
version or choose any number in between.
To go with the camera, you will need a selfie stick,
and there's no need really to spend a lot of money on this.
In fact, the free one that came with the camera is perfectly fine.
In fact, this is my selfie stick of choice
when travelling or when I'm just doing day-to-day filming since it extends out to around
a meter and the quality is also really good.
I know there's the temptation to buy and bring more
expensive gear and selfie sticks, but when you're travelling, there's a higher margin for error
and risk, which is why going with the cheaper alternatives is going to be a better choice.
Another fantastic accessory you'll want to consider for your travels is the power selfie stick,
which has power built into the actual selfie stick, as well as recording buttons on the handle.
This will extend the battery life of your camera by two to three times,
which is especially handy on those really long travel days
where you might not have time to charge your camera.
You'll probably want to bring a normal power bank with you as well, but that's optional.
The best 360 camera clamp is a great travel accessory because it basically gives you a lot
of versatility for mounting your selfie stick to any place you like.
Another worthwhile accessory
is the Insta360 quick reader, which allows you to insert your camera's SD card into it,
and then it plugs directly into your phone,
meaning you can edit your shots faster since
the SD card's connected directly to the phone,
which makes the app faster, and it also means
your camera doesn't need to be on and draining battery while you're doing your editing.
If you're looking for a small camera pouch to carry your accessories, I love these
Think Tank Cable Management bags, which I've been personally using for a long time.
I think I bought these around five years ago,
and they're such quality that they don't break.
They've got this clear window
so you can see exactly what's inside, and they come in
multiple sizes depending on how much gear you're bringing.
I'll link all of these accessories below.
Now, whether you want to bring more or less than this is up to you. They're not all necessary.
At the bare minimum, you'll just need to bring your camera and SD card and a selfie stick.
Next, you want to make sure you pick the right activities for filming in 360 and
knowing what is going to work well and what's not.
Since 360 cameras shoot wide-angle shots,
sometimes this is perfect for certain activities where you really need that wide-angle perspective,
and other times it's really not. 360 cameras are not a one-size-fits-all tool,
and if you're focusing on anything far away in the distance and you want to capture it with
any level of detail, then I'd still recommend using a phone or another kind of camera that
has more resolution in one direction only.
I've just come back from an amazing trip to
Queenstown in New Zealand, and when I was there, I shot with both my X3 and my phone because certain
situations required one, and other ones required the other.
The kinds of scenes that work well shot
with the 360 camera are ones where the action is close to you and the camera can easily see it a
few meters away, or if you have an epic location that truly has 360-degree views.
Both of these things have potential to make for amazing reframed 360 videos
but again, if you need more quality in
one direction and the activities you're filming are far away, like if you're doing sightseeing
or you just need a long lens perspective, then consider using your phone or another camera.
So when I went to Queenstown, I deliberately chose my activities to be 360-friendly.
The first one was Milford Sound, which has truly 360-degree views.
The next was a bunch of fun activities around Queenstown
where I knew the action was going to be close to me.
And the third one was Mount Cook,
a place where you've got both 360-degree views and some great hiking
shots to be had in front of amazing backgrounds. Once you've chosen the right activities to film
in 360, next you're going to need to refine your shooting techniques.
Often when you're travelling,
you don't have as much time to stop and think about what kind of camera setups you're going
to achieve while you're there. You've got to be fast-paced and often make quick decisions.
So learning how to adapt to a changing and unfamiliar environment is really important.
The most fail-safe way to do this is keeping your camera on a selfie stick. In the vast
majority of places you visit, shooting with your camera handheld is a surefire way to capture both
you and your environment to be used either in the same shot or completely separately.
And for the majority of shots, that is what you're going for, so there's no need to set up tripods,
monopods, or any other kind of complicated camera setup when you can just keep things
simple and shoot with a selfie stick.
And I'm just looking back at the shots I took.
I think I got around 40 of them in total. I would say around 35 of the 40 were taken with the
camera on the selfie stick. My next shooting tip is to give your shots a sense of movement
with either you moving through your location or capturing things moving around you.
This will make your shots far more engaging and cinematic.
If you are capturing a travel vlog where you're featuring
in the video, then try to keep the camera close to your face.
The ideal distance is between one and three feet,
just depending on how prominently you want to feature in the shot. If you do want to
feature prominently, hold it around a foot away. If you want to showcase the background behind you,
then by all means, extend the camera an arm's length away from you.
Also, if you have the luxury of time,
then try a bunch of different angles. The first angle you shoot won't always be the best,
so try the camera in a few different positions: in front of your face, at an arm's length away
from you, above you, to the side. If you are at an amazing location, then it will definitely be
worth capturing multiple angles so you can find the winning clip later on when you're editing.
I'd also recommend shooting as soon and as quickly as you can at certain locations
because you never know when the weather's going to change. One minute it's sunny and blue skies,
the next it's grey skies and bucketing down, and you have no control over the weather, but you do
have control over how quickly you shoot. So don't wait around. And that happened to me here at this
amazing view over Queenstown, where I was able to capture a few shots while it was still clear. But
literally 20 minutes later, a snowstorm started, and suddenly that amazing view became completely white.
And to be fair, this can also cause some fun spontaneous shots. Sometimes your plan B,
like here walking through the snowstorm, can add a fun and memorable element to your vlog.
Now, an effect I need to mention when it comes to travel is hyperlapses.
Hyperlapses look great in any location, but especially when you're travelling through amazing scenery.
More often than not, it's going to look amazing sped up and reframed into a hyperlapse.
So I'd always recommend any time you travel, shoot at least one hyperlapse
To do it, record 360 video with
your camera for at least five minutes, or if you want to give yourself more flexibility later on,
you can go up to 10 or even 20 minutes. Then in the Insta360 app, speed it up to 16 to 64 times,
add the motion blur effect, and voila, you've got an amazing hyperlapse.
I'd also recommend not shooting everything. While I was travelling, I did notice a few other people
with X3s, and they all seemed to be filming everything that they were doing, literally every
moment of their vacation they were filming. And I can only imagine the headache it would be to sort
through those thousands of clips and hundreds of hours of footage to find a few good moments.
So I'd really recommend only shooting when you have to to make editing much easier later on.
If you plan on capturing sound and dialogue in your travel vlog, then the inbuilt microphones of
most Insta360 cameras will be good enough. It's not going to be amazing quality, but it will be
good enough, assuming you're not at too loud of a location. If you do plan on talking a lot
in your vlog, that's when you want to consider using the invisible microphone setup that can
be achieved with most recent Insta360 cameras and the Rode Wireless Go microphone system.
If you want to learn how to do that, I go into more depth about how to record sound properly inside
my 360 video 101 course, as well as hundreds of other shooting and editing techniques that
I've refined over the years to help me create amazing travel videos in any and every type of
location around the world. So if you want to get instant access to my past eight-plus years of 360
video knowledge and become a better content creator in just seven days, then follow the
link below to learn more about 360 video 101. The next aspect you need to consider with your
travel vlog is finding the best and easiest editing workflow. When you're at home, you've
got the luxury of a desktop computer and all the time in the world. But when you're travelling,
you don't have either of those things. So to really get the most out of your edits, you're
going to need to adapt to a mobile workflow. Now, if you really want, you can bring a laptop
with you. I've got to say, I am loving my new MacBook Air 13-inch; it's fantastic,
really good tool for basic computer work while you're travelling. But to be honest with you,
I didn't use it at all for video editing.
This is simply because the Insta360 mobile app is
so streamlined for mobile editing that there's no need to overcomplicate things and create a
longer workflow importing files to your computer, stitching, exporting; there's just a lot to do
while you're travelling that you don't need to do on a bigger device. Instead, I'd recommend
mastering the Insta360 mobile app, which has so many features, so many great edits you can do
to your footage on the go that it negates the need for a computer while you're travelling.
So, the workflow that worked best for me was using my iPhone with the Insta360 quick reader,
and that was perfectly fine for getting out some quick social media shots before I returned home
at the end of my trip to edit properly on my computer. Although a great new addition to the
app worth mentioning is that you can now export at 4K quality with a 125-megabits-a-second bit rate,
which is great for maximizing video quality.
Step five, and this isn't so much a shooting
or editing tip, but it's more of a trap that up-and-coming content creators find themselves
in every time they go travelling, and that is becoming so consumed with content creation
that you're not experiencing the experience that you're filming.
We've all done this before.
"Wow, this location's so amazing, I need to get the money shot at all costs."
But in pursuit of the money shot, you don't take the time to be present and appreciate it with your own eyes.
And often, that's why you go travelling, to have great experiences,
to be present with new environments. And while capturing your travels is fantastic,
it's also important to know when to put the camera down and experience the experience
instead of just capturing the experience. If you have any 360 video travel tips to add,
let me know down below.
Now, before you set off on your epic adventure,
now that you've got some of the technical stuff accounted for,
next you're going to need some creative inspiration because
no matter how technically competent you are, without being able to combine that with creativity,
your shots can still fall flat.
So check out this video here to see 20 awesome creative shots
that I got on my trip to Queenstown that you can easily recreate on your next adventure.

खुलता नहीं था। तो एक बार टूटा तो पूरा
कैमरा ही गया। बट इस बार दोनों कंपनियों
ने अपना नया लेटेस्ट 360 कैमरा ल्च कर
दिया। Insta 360 ने X6 ल्च किया है। शेप
एंड साइज को थोड़ा सा छोटा कर दिया। तो अब
हेलमेट में माउंट करना और कहीं भी कैरी
करना काफी ज्यादा इजी हो जाता है। 8K50 का
भी ऑप्शन है और साथ ही साथ रिमूवर लेंस तो
आपका X5 से ही आ गया था। DJI ने भी फिर
Osm 360 ल्च किया तो उन्होंने कहा कि आप
8K50 दे रहे हो तो चलो हम 8K60 दे रहे
हैं। बिफोर बाइंग अ 360 आप लोगों को एक
नॉलेज होना चाहिए कि एक एक्शन कैमरा एक
360 दोनों ही डिफरेंट चीज है। एक
मोटोव्लॉगर सोचता है कि हम एक 360 कैमरा
ले रहे हैं। सारी चीजें इसी से कर लेंगे।
क्योंकि ये हर तरफ का एंगल रिकॉर्ड कर
सकता है। इसको क्यों ही ले? अगर एक्शन
कैमरा से आप कुछ भी चीज रिकॉर्ड करते हो
तो इसको डायरेक्टली फुटेज को डाउनलोड कर
सकते हो। 360 में ऐसा नहीं है आपको
एक्सपोर्ट करना पड़ेगा। पूरा एंगल चूस
करना पड़ेगा। और आप लोग में से बहुत लोग
बोलेंगे भाई कि AI का ऑप्शन आ गया है। भाई
AI का ऑप्शन X3 से अवेलेबल है। वो ऑटो
रिफ्रेमिंग करके आपको दे देता है। लेकिन
एक एआई और एक ह्यूमन बिल्कुल ही अपोजिट
थिंग है भाई।

caption_lines.text: a while ago insta 360 reached out to me
to see if I could test their new camera
the insta 360 X3 to see if it's any good
for hiking and I know it's going to
sound pretty bold but after testing it
for 2 months I think that currently this
is the best action camera for filming
stuff outdoors and let me tell you why
the main idea behind it is that it has a
360° camera it's able to do this by
having a very wide lens on each side and
then automatically stitching it all
together in post it also deletes the
camera body and the selfie stick from
the video so that in the end you get a
clean 360 video from all sides the main
problem with normal action cameras and
dslrs is that I always have to frame the
shot perfectly otherwise it doesn't end
up looking the way that I want it to
look so you can just hold the camera in
front of you and later when editing you
can rotate it so that it faces towards
you away from you or in any other
direction the most common shot that I'm
making with this camera is by holding it
in front of me and then talking to the
camera as I'm walking the footage is
automatically stabilized so I don't
really have to worry about holding it
very steadily in my arm and in my
opinion the footage just looks good you
can also extend the invisible selfie
stick and hold it in front of you or
move it around or you could even take it
over your shoulder to the back to create
these cool third person shots in my
opinion it's really useful if you want
to show the conditions of the trail or
if you want to show the surrounding
views in general you can also use it as
a regular camera by putting it on a
tripod and then putting it on the ground
and walking past it the main difference
here is that later when editing you can
rotate the camera so that it looks like
someone is moving the camera as you walk
past it by setting it up on a tripod you
can also create a moving time lapse with
it again I want to emphasize that this
is achieved without any fancy equipment
it's all done in post just by changing
the angle of the shot slightly within a
few seconds if you hold the camera
steady in front of you and then continue
walking like that for about 1 minute
then you can speed it all up in post and
create a very cool looking hyperlapse
another cool feature of the X3 is the
POV shots simply put the camera in your
mouth and continue walking as normally
or you can also put it on the invisible
selfie stick and then put it inside your
backpack I found it to be really useful
for showcasing the steepest and the most
dangerous parts of the trail you might
have already seen this on your Instagram
feed because it's pretty popular now but
you can create amazing drone like shots
without using a drone you can do it with
the 3 m long extended selfie stick
simply put the camera on the end extend
it to the maximum and then walk around
while holding the extended selfie stick
in your hand and lastly when you reach
the top you can connect the tripods to
the invisible selfie stick and create a
bullet time shot this is a very unique
and cool shot that shows a perspective
of the surrounding area the camera
itself is pretty small and it easily
fits in your pocket it's also waterproof
in up to 10 m of depth which is really
useful for the outdoors because you
don't have to worry about it getting wet
when you're filming in Rain you should
always shoot in five .7k quality if you
want the best possible footage now 5.7k
sounds like a lot and it actually is for
example my DSLR can only shoot in up to
4K quality the difference here is that
the 5.7k resolution is spread out over
all of the
360° so later when editing the video
when you're cutting it down smaller the
end quality actually isn't 5.7k it's
much smaller in good light conditions
the shots coming out from the X3 come
out very crisp it only starts to
struggle a bit in low light conditions
but even then I would say that the
footage still looks pretty good when
shooting a time lapse it's even able to
shoot in 8k quality so the time lapses
end up very highend it has a built-in
microphone that sounds pretty good if
you aren't filming in very windy
conditions like I am right now but just
like with any camera the audio from the
built-in microphone becomes pretty bad
if if you film it on exposed ridges with
a lot of
wind it's getting pretty
winky so if you want to be recording

time kit which I've linked out to in the

fingerprints with the tripod you can add

127 G but if you want to film those sick

be the never-ending story for us
surfers.
There are waves all over the world we
dream of being able to surf one day.
From remote islands in Indonesia, the
long perfect point breaks in Africa,

However,
there is one wave many of us have no
interest in ever surfing.
But, we all wish to see it in person.
You're kidding me. Insane. This is nuts.

powerful waves on the planet and more
recently famous for being the surf
destination in the 2024 Paris Olympic
Games. Even though it's located all the
way in the middle of the Pacific Ocean
on the island of Tahiti. This week, I'm
here to document local surf legend and
GoPro athlete Tereva David to showcase
what a day at Teahupo'o looks like from
his perspective. And today, I'm bringing
you along for the journey.
Another beautiful morning in Tahiti.
This is
unreal.
Where are we going?

Let's get it.

caption_lines.text: Do you want to add stats like speed,
heart rate, and power to your cycling
videos? It's very simple. This is how I
do it. I use a Insta360 GO 3S or any
Insta360 camera and a COROS Dura bike
computer. I start the Insta360 GO 3S
recording from my phone to have precise
timestamps and simply record the ride on
the COROS Dura computer. When you're
finished, open up the Insta360 app, go
to the clip you want, select stats,
stats source, COROS, and bam, magically
all these stats will appear. Super easy
and seamless and your video is ready to
be posted with all these overlays.

clips.title: Insta360 X6 vs X5 vs DJI Osmo 360: THIS is the BEST 360 Camera!
comment_snippets: The X6 is a great camera! What do you think of the X6? There's a limited number of Creator Gift Packs available. If you'd like to take advantage of this offer, use the following link: https://bit.ly/X6_MountMedia
Waiting for Osmo 360 | |
Thanks for the very detailed review!

caption_lines.text: The Insta360 X6 is here. And this clip was created automatically by the camera and the app.
No reframing, no editing – Zero Edit – one of the X6’s particular strengths. And the result is good,
significantly better than with previous tools. The X6 features three different automated editing
functions. I’ll show you how they work a little later. But apart from that, what else is new with
the X6, and just how good is the camera really? To find out, I compared the X6 to the best 360
cameras currently available. The X5 and the DJI Osmo360. The Osmo360 2 is due to be released soon,
but only in China. There is no information yet regarding an international release, and
a launch in the US is unlikely – the X5 and the Osmo360 are therefore currently the best cameras
for comparison.There are 10 categories that are important for the quality of a 360 camera. Take
a close look at all the categories, because there are a few interesting surprises. At the end, I’ll
tell you whether I think an upgrade makes sense and what special offers are currently available.
The X6 was provided to me by Insta360 for testing purposes, but this video does not
include any additional paid sponsorship! For the first time in a long while, Insta360
has completely redesigned the body of its 360 camera with the X6. The X6 no longer has that very
elongated shape. It’s slightly wider than the X5, but significantly shorter. In terms of form alone,
it’s a compromise between the X5 and the Osmo360. It still works well with a selfie stick, and the
slightly shorter form factor is better suited for mounting on a helmet or chest mount. In terms of
volume, it’s about the same size as the Osmo360 and slightly smaller than the X5. At 195 grams,
it weighs slightly more than the Osmo360 and just a bit less than the X5. Especially when
compared to the Osmo360, the X6 has a few key advantages. It features a significantly larger,
high-quality OLED-display. The X5’s display is similar in size, but its vertical format makes
it less suitable for single-lens shots. To make room for the X6’s large OLED display, the physical
buttons were moved to the side. In their place, two virtual buttons were added at the bottom
edge. Similar to modern smartphones, they provide haptic feedback when pressed. If needed, you can
even turn the entire screen into a record button. The display and camera feel very high-quality,
and the virtual buttons work very well—so well, in fact, that I hardly ever used the physical buttons
during my test recordings. Of course, that will be different in the winter when wearing gloves. And,
of course, the lens can be replaced on your own. Similar to the X5, there’s a Lens Replacement Kit
that lets you replace a damaged lens on your own. And that’s important: even though Insta360 says
the lenses have been reinforced and are supposed to be significantly less prone to scratches,
the protruding lenses are still a weak point of a 360 camera, since they can be easily damaged.
What I also like is that replacing a lens is now much easier than on the X5. And the lenses are
certainly one of the Osmo360’s biggest weaknesses in this comparison. On the one hand, you can’t
replace them yourself; you have to send the camera in if they’re damaged. On the other hand, the Osmo
360’s lenses can fog up, for example when there are extreme temperature differences, such as when
used in water. I also ran a similar test with the X6, and unlike the Osmo 360, it doesn’t fog up.
Incidentally, the X6 is waterproof to a depth of up to 20 metres without an additional dive case.
That’s more than the X5 or the Osmo360, which is only waterproof to a depth of 10 metres.
It all looks good—smaller, very well-built, a high-quality display. But ultimately,
what matters most is the image quality and how the footage looks.
Whenever a new camera is released, there’s always discussion about sponsored reviews. For me,
the solution is quite simple: I’ll explain the key differences to you and show you several
longer comparison clips that are unedited except for reframing. This way, you’ll be
able to form your own independent opinion. The X6 features two all-new 1/1.1-inch
sensors and improved chips. The new sensors are completely new square Sony sensors,
designed specifically for Insta360. At 1/1.1 inches, the new sensors are the
same size as those in the Osmo360 and larger than the X5’s sensors, which measure 1/1.28 inches.
When we compare the footage from the X6 with that from the X5, only minor differences are noticeable
at first glance. Both clips were reframed using the Field of View Mega. Interestingly,
the X5’s field of view is slightly wider. But there are a few other interesting differences.
The colors differ slightly. Especially here in the shots of this mountain meadow, the
X6’s colors appear more natural—they more closely match reality—the meadow is greener in reality,
just as it appears on the X6, and does not have the orange tones of the X5. Here’s a comparison
shot I took with an iPhone. But that’s perhaps the most noticeable difference in the colors. Much
greater and more significant are the differences in dynamic range. Compared to the X5, the X6 has a
clearly improved dynamic range, and highlights are preserved much better. You can see that,
for example, here in the background with the sun. And even more so in this shot here in the office.
You can clearly see how the details in the window are more blown out on the X5. Or in this example
with the castle. And there’s something else that stands out here. In some cases, the X5
shows unsightly blue lens flares. That’s not the case with the X6. In my opinion, the X6 comes
with very high-quality lenses, and I’ve actually never noticed any unsightly lens flares, even when
shooting against the sun. For me personally, this is one of the most important improvements in image
quality on the X6. By the way, there are no longer any settings for Adaptive Tone or HDR on the X6.
I see hardly any differences when it comes to detail—here’s a comparison at 400%. Both shots
show a similar level of detail. How does it compare to the Osmo360? Compared to the X5,
the Osmo360 produces shots with slightly less saturation. For these comparison shots,
I also used the standard field of view on both cameras. And these comparison shots don’t look all
that different either. It’s interesting that the Osmo360 often uses more magenta tones than the X6.
That wasn’t always the case in comparisons between DJI and Insta360 cameras. You can also see that in
this shot of the meadow on the mountain. The X6’s shot renders the meadow significantly greener than
the Osmo360’s. Sometimes, when shooting against the light, the Osmo360 tends to underexpose the
shot slightly. This makes the subject appear somewhat underexposed, as in this shot here. But
overall, both cameras take very good shots. The Osmo360’s dynamic range is better than that of the
X5 and very similar to that of the X6. There are only very minor differences. In this shot taken
here in the office, the X6 performs only slightly better. The black T-shirt shows slightly more
detail in the X6’s shot, and the highlights are also preserved slightly better. Similar to the X5,
the Osmo360 can also have issues with lens flares in certain situations—and in this comparison,
you can see that the X6 handles lens flares significantly better than the Osmo360.
There’s one important topic we haven’t even touched on yet: Just like the Osmo360, the X6
can shoot in 8K at up to 50 frames per second. The X5 offers a maximum frame rate of 30 frames per
second in 8K. This is a significant upgrade, especially for those who prefer a slightly
smoother, more natural look. On the other hand, I’m a bit disappointed with the 360 slow-motion
footage. The X6 shoots in 4K at up to 100 frames per second, just like the Osmo360. The X5 is the
only one of the three cameras capable of shooting in 4K at 120 frames per second. On top of that,
I find that the X6’s image quality in 4K100 isn’t optimal, and that the X5, in particular, produces
better slow-motion footage in 4K. We’ll see that, fortunately, when it comes to slow motion, the X6
has a significant advantage in Single Lens mode. And the X6 has another feature that’s been long
overdue for Insta360. It supports 10-bit Log recording, even in 8K. The X5 does have a LOG
color profile, but only in 8-bit. Furthermore, the X5’s LOG profile isn’t available in 8K—only
in 5.7K. The Osmo360, on the other hand, also features a 10-bit Log profile that lets you
shoot in 8K. However, this is D-LOG M, and as you can see here, D-LOG M is nowhere near as flat as
the X6’s new Log profile. As a result, the dynamic range of the X6’s Log profile is better than that
of D-LOG M on the Osmo360. I converted these two clips using the manufacturers’ LUTs, and
unlike the Osmo360, the X6 produces a very neutral image that’s well-suited for further processing.
But the X6 has another important advantage when it comes to color profiles. It’s the first 360 camera
capable of capturing 8K 360 footage in 10-bit HDR Dolby Vision. This means footage where,
in particular, the highlights can be displayed much brighter. To take advantage of this, however,
you’ll need an HDR-capable display, such as the screen of a modern smartphone or a modern TV. As
you can see here in this direct comparison, the HDR footage has significantly more contrast and
looks more realistic. As my YouTube review isn’t an HDR video, I can’t show the full
dynamic range. But I get the impression that HDR videos sometimes look a bit overexposed,
even when viewed on a smartphone. Insta360 could do with making some improvements in this area.
You can reframe your 360 Dolby Vision video as usual and export it as an HDR Dolby Vision video.
This is a great feature for anyone who frequently watches their videos on a smartphone or TV.
The X6 has also made slight improvements in low-light performance. The X6 is the
best 360 camera to date for shooting in low light. Similar to the X5 and the Osmo 360,
it has its own dedicated shooting mode for use in low light. However,
the difference compared to the X5 isn’t that big. Especially considering the size of its sensor,
the X5 already takes very good shots in low light. It’s also extremely dark here. Actually,
you shouldn’t really be filming in such lighting conditions. But this scenario is
simply better suited for comparison shots and to better highlight the differences. As I said,
the difference compared to the X5’s footage really isn’t that big. The X6’s footage has slightly less
image noise and is a bit sharper. And here, too, you can see that the issues with lens flares have
been resolved. The same applies when compared to the Osmo360. The Osmo360’s footage is darker and
lacks some detail. As mentioned at the beginning, the Osmo360 has sensors the same size as the X6.
This means that the performance of the Pure Video mode is simply the deciding factor,
as was also evident from the X5’s good results. But you can’t say that the X6’s lead is huge.
Interestingly, the differences in Single Lens mode are perhaps greater overall than in 360
mode. The X6 clearly performs better here. This is true both when compared to the Osmo360 and
when compared to the X5. The colors in the X6’s recordings look better, and they also show more
detail. And that brings us to a topic where the X6 has made great progress: the single-lens mode.
As we’ve just seen, the X6 clearly performs best in low-light conditions among all three cameras
in Single Lens mode. But that’s not the only improvement Insta360 has made in Single Lens
mode. All three cameras can capture flat footage with just one lens, which you no longer need to
reframe. And just like the Osmo360, the X6 can now also capture flat footage in 5K at up to 60 frames
per second. On the X5, the maximum is 4K60. As you can see here on the camera, with the X6 you can
set the field of view relatively freely in Single Lens mode and also enable distortion correction.
That’s really cool – the footage in Single Lens mode looks good, but I’ve also noticed that the
Osmo 360 and the X5 apply more HDR processing. The highlights can blow out a bit more quickly
on the X6 in Single Lens mode. I don’t know if that might change with a future firmware update.
what I’m really excited about is that with the X6 in Single Lens mode, you can now also shoot
slow-motion footage in 4K at up to 120 frames per second. This is also possible with the Osmo 360,
but only in the extremely wide ‘Boost’ mode. With the X6, 4K120 is available in Single
Lens mode regardless of the field of view. This means the X6 is increasingly capable of
replacing a traditional action camera. High-quality slow-motion footage has
been one of the few remaining exclusive features of a standard action camera.
Of course, all three cameras still have several other shooting modes, such as for time-lapses
or hyperlapses. Just like the Osmo360, the X6 can take 360 photos with up to 120 megapixels.
I’ve done a comparison of a few photos here in the office, as many people are interested in
indoor 360° photos. This is a heavily cropped version of the photos. Unlike the Osmo360,
the X6 has a significantly higher dynamic range, also because it features an HDR mode. The level
of detail is also slightly better than on the Osmo360. Compared to the X5, there’s a
noticeable improvement in detail, partly because the X5’s photo has significantly fewer megapixels.
There have also been improvements to the Bullet Time mode. The Bullet Time mode is
now available for the first time in 8K at up to 100 frames per second. But I find
the Instaframe mode—which is exclusive to the X6 and X5—much more interesting. In Instaframe mode,
you can select a subject and track it directly in the camera, much like you would with a gimbal
camera. You’ll then get a perfectly reframed flat clip in 4K with the “Invisible Selfie
Stick” effect. No more editing required. The tracking and reframing are therefore performed
directly in the camera. If needed, you can also simultaneously record a 360 backup clip in 8K,
which you can reframe yourself—just in case you’re not satisfied with the flat clip.
Simultaneous recording in 4K and 8K—that’s not possible with the X5. When recording a
flat clip and a 360 clip at the same time, the resolution on the X5 must be reduced to 1080.
And that brings us to a topic that sets the X6 and Insta360 apart. The goal is to increasingly
relieve users of the need to edit and reframe their footage. After all, reframing is still
considered the biggest drawback of a 360 camera. To take the reframing off the user’s hands, the X6
supports a new, completely revamped Autoedit feature in the app. You select a few clips,
and the app does the rest. Until now, the results were rather average. That has now actually been
improved. By the way, the intro clip was created using the new Auto Edit feature.
But there are two more new features. With the new AI Director feature,
the X6 analyzes all clips recorded that day at the end of the day and while charging,
identifies highlights, and automatically transfers a custom-generated daily vlog to
your smartphone—all fully automatically—you don’t actually have to do anything except activate the
feature. Everything runs on the camera and app. No upload to the cloud is required for this feature.
With AI Director, you don’t even have to select the clips yourself. This feature automatically
compiles a montage of some of the best shots of the day, which you can share straight away.
In contrast, the new cloud features, Moments & Moments Pro, which work in conjunction with Google
Gemini, are quite different. After you’ve uploaded your clips to the cloud, Moments Pro becomes a
kind of personal editor. The clips are analyzed, and various editing schemes are suggested. You
can then select different tags or protagonists and start the edit. This process takes place entirely
in the cloud, and you’ll be notified as soon as the video is ready. The feature is interesting and
works well, but there’s a catch—you’ll naturally need a cloud subscription to take advantage of it.
depending on the keyword, it can also pick out key scenes from older,
perhaps even forgotten, recordings. All three features represent an upgrade
to the previous AutoEdit function. Generally speaking, in my opinion, it’s not about getting
the best possible result from your footage. Rather, it’s about getting a good montage of
your footage quickly and easily, without having to do the editing yourself if you don’t feel
like it. And the results can be really cool! But that isn’t a feature exclusive to the X6.
all the new automated editing features will also be available for the X5. If you’d like to find
out more about the new Autoedit features, have a look at my tutorial on the subject.
I’ll include a link to it in the description. With all these new features and the smaller
form factor, the question of recording time naturally arises. So how long can the X6 shoot,
and are there any overheating issues? I ran a test here in the office at 8K30 at
a warm 26 degrees Celsius and without any airflow. Under these unfavorable conditions, there were no
overheating issues whatsoever, and the X6 was able to shoot for an incredible 2 hours and 38 minutes.
That’s 1 hour and 10 minutes longer than the Osmo360 and the X5. Only the X5 had overheating
issues under these conditions and shut down after 56 minutes due to overheating. Of course,
it’s worth noting that in real-world use and with airflow, none of the three cameras will have
overheating problems. For most people, overheating will therefore remain more of a theoretical issue.
But Insta360 has gotten everything right this time when it comes to overheating and battery life.
To capture shots like this one or this underwater shot, a 360 camera requires
very specific accessories. And in this regard, not only the X6 but also the X5 have a major—if
not decisive—advantage. It’s true that all sticks and mounts are compatible with all 360
cameras. But Insta360 is the only manufacturer so far to offer an Invisible Dive case for its
360 cameras. And only with such a dive case can you take 360° shots underwater, since underwater
shots place entirely different demands on lens stitching. Unfortunately, the Dive Case for
the X6 wasn’t available at the time of my test, which is why you’re seeing footage from the X5
here. But a Dive Case for the X6 will be available soon. However, a dive case is now also available
for the X6. Apart from that, there are several remote controls, ND filters and other special
mounts and accessories available for the X6. And have you seen this: the Luna Ultra’s POV
Head Tracker? It’s worn like a headset and is also compatible with the X6. When using the
Instframe mode, The framing automatically adjusts to the movements of your head.
Personally, I wouldn't want to do without the DiveCase. For me personally,
the lack of an Invisible Dive Case is one of the Osmo360’s major weaknesses
I know that many users aren't particularly interested in audio quality. But Insta360 has been
constantly working to further improve the audio quality of its cameras—and the X6 is no exception.
The X6 features a new Windproof 360 microphone. The camera has microphone openings on all sides
that are protected from the wind. And of course, the X6 also includes the excellent
Voice Enhancement mode, which effectively filters out background noise. But of course,
for even better audio quality, there are external microphones available for all
three cameras. The best choice for the X6 is definitely the relatively new Mic Pro.
What else is important? What other differences are there between the three cameras? The X6 also
comes with a very special feature: 3D Spatial Capture. Put simply, this is a technique that
creates a 3D model from a video or photo – a 3D model within which you can move around freely.
This is a particularly important upgrade for anyone who uses their 360° camera professionally,
for example for virtual tours. You don’t just get a photo where you can look around freely;
you get a high-quality 3D model in which you can move around freely. For example,
a house that you can explore virtually and freely. For many people, this is certainly a very cool
feature. Unfortunately, 3D Spatial Capture is not available in the US at launch for technical
reasons. However, this is set to change. And for me, very important:
Unlike the X5, the X6 finally has internal storage. At 47 gigabytes, it’s only about
half as much as the Osmo 360, but it’s enough in case you forget your SD card. And, of course,
the apps are important, too. Especially when compared to other manufacturers, the Insta360 apps
are still the best in terms of feature set. This applies to both the smartphone app and the desktop
app. That said, you can of course also reframe your clips quite well with the DJI Mimo app.
I think the X6 has turned out to be a fantastic camera that gets almost everything right. And
the new AutoEdit features and 3D Spatial Capture expand the functionality of a 360-degree camera.
Of course, that comes at a price. The Insta360 X6 starts at $699 in the U.S. and at €699 in Europe.
That’s the only real downside of the X6 in this comparison, since the X5 is already available
starting at $550 or €590 in Europe. The Osmo360 is similarly priced, but you can find it cheaper from
third-party retailers like Amazon. You’ll find links to all three cameras in the description
below. If you use the link for the X6, You'll also receive an exclusive creator gift pack. It's
supposed to be an extremely useful Double Lens KIT that lets you replace two damaged lenses.
So check out the offer—it's a limited-time deal, so you'll want to act fast if you're interested.
If you have an older camera, there’s also a trade-in program you can take advantage of. This
applies to DJI and GoPro cameras as well. I’ll include a link to this in the description too.
So what would I recommend? In my opinion, the X6 has turned out to be a perfect 360 camera. It has
hardly any flaws, and aside from slow-motion in 360 mode, there’s hardly anything more you could
ask for right now. I really like the new lenses and the fact that all the lens flare issues have
been fixed. The new automated editing options are cool, too. It’s basically a flawless camera,
though it doesn’t have any absolutely standout killer features. If you’re buying a new camera
and can afford it, I’d go with the X6. But if you want to save some money, the X5 and the Osmo360
are still very good alternatives. Give me a like as feedback if you found this video interesting.
A detailed beginner’s tutorial on the X6 will follow soon. So stay tuned, and see you next time.
