caption_lines.text: In a previous video I tested the Insta360 magnetic backpack holster with my X5.
While it's mainly designed to let you
quickly stash your camera while you're on the move,
I found it also works surprisingly well as
a POV mount when the camera is holstered.
And since then I've been using it a lot,
not just with the X5,
but also with my DJI Osmo 360.
But recently I came across a popular
YouTube video where the creator had their Insta360
mounted on a peak design capture clip, and
that got me thinking I already have one of
those from back in my peak design phase, so
I dug it out and decided to see which setup
really works better for POV shooting with a 360 camera.
That's exactly what I'm testing in this
video, the peak design capture clip
vs the Insta360 backpack holster.
I'll be comparing them head to head with
both the Insta360 X5 and DJI Osmo 360, looking
at things like usability, framing, build quality, comfort and flexibility.
And just a quick note, while I'm using the
peak design capture clip, my findings should
apply to similar backpack clips from the likes of PGY Tech, Falcam and Ulanzi.
Let's start with ease of use. Both systems
work by clipping onto one of your backpack
straps to serve as the mounting point for
your camera. On my North Face Recon, which
has fairly thick straps, I had to push
pretty hard to get the Insta360 magnetic holster clipped on.
By comparison, the peak design
capture clip was a little easier to secure,
so it's the better option for those with even thicker straps.
Once mounted, the big usability difference is how your camera attaches.
The Insta360 holster gives you a small magnetic connector
that goes between your camera and selfie stick.
With that in place, the stick
will click into place on the holster and to
take it out, you just twist the grip and it
releases instantly. The capture clip on the
other hand uses a base plate that screws into
the bottom of your camera. That plate
slides into the clip until it locks with a click
and you release it by pressing the quick
release button and sliding it out. So in both cases,
mounting and detaching the camera is a
quick and smooth process, but detaching from the
holster is slightly quicker thanks to the twist to release mechanism.
Another advantage of the holster, when you take the camera out,
it's already on the selfie stick, ready for handheld shooting.
With the capture clip,
you're just left holding the camera on a base plate,
not ideal if you want to quickly switch to
stick mounted filming, which is usually the
preferred way to film with 360 cameras.
Now since the Peak Design Plate is Arca Swiss compatible,
you could potentially rig up a more complex solution,
but the Insta360 holster offers the cleanest solution.
Now let's compare some actual POV footage.
Even though both mounts attach to your backpack strap,
the height and orientation of the camera end up a little different,
which affects your framing.
And the most noticeable difference is how much of your head creeps into the shot.
With the Insta360 X5, the capture clip pushes the camera slightly further out,
which meant less of my head showed up at wider angles.
The holster by comparison keeps the camera closer to the body,
so a bit more of my head ended up in the frame.
With the Osmo360, it's almost the opposite.
Because the camera is shorter, the holster positions the lens lower,
which meant less of my head was visible at wider angles.
On the other hand, the capture clip showed more of my head,
but gave me a clearer over the shoulder shot.
That said, take these findings with a grain of salt,
because with the capture clip especially, placement makes a big difference.
What I just showed you was with the clip mounted high on the strap.
Later, when I tried moving it lower for my Osmo360,
I got less head in the frame at the cost of some rear visibility.
So your exact results will depend on where you mount it,
and even your own body shape.
One final difference with regard to framing
is how the mounts themselves show up in the frame.
With the holster, the mount becomes pretty noticeable if you pan down.
This is barely an issue with the backpack clip,
where you really have to go out of your way
in order to be able to see the backpack clip itself.
When it comes to build quality and reliability,
the Peak Design Capture Clip feels like the more robust option.
It's a well-established accessory with years of proven use,
and it's even rated to handle over 200 pounds or 90kg.
That gives you a lot of confidence if
you're planning to use it in rougher conditions.
The Insta360 Magnetic Holster, on the other hand, is newer.
While it works fine for now,
the magnetic connection could potentially be more vulnerable
to wear or malfunction over time,
compared to the simple slot in design of the capture clip.
I also noticed the holster holds the camera and stick a little more loosely,
so there's a bit of give if you bump it around.
So for more demanding activities,
I trust the capture clip slightly more.
But for day-to-day filming or lighter use,
the magnetic holster holds up just fine.
In terms of comfort, the capture clip has the edge.
With the magnetic holster, you're not just carrying the camera,
you're also carrying the entire selfie stick on your strap.
That means a fairly long grip is always hanging off your shoulder.
It's not a huge deal, but if you want the
least obstruction to your upper body movement,
the capture clip definitely feels less intrusive.
As for looks, I don't think there's a huge difference.
With the holster, it's obvious you've just got a camera mounted on your backpack.
With the capture clip, it's less clear
exactly what's sticking out from your shoulder,
which may naturally draw more attention.
Where the capture clip really pulls ahead though,
is the part that stays on your strap.
Its slim, low profile design means you can leave it on your backpack permanently
and basically forget it's there.
The holster by contrast has a much bulkier footprint,
something I'm more tempted to remove if I'm not actively using it.
Finally, let's talk about flexibility.
Neither of these backpack mounts were
specifically designed for POV filming with a 360 camera,
so their functionality extends beyond that.
The Insta360 holster is definitely more specialised.
It's really meant for action cameras or 360 cameras mounted on selfie sticks,
and that's about it.
If that's what you need, it does the job very well,
but I can't think of many use cases outside of that.
The capture clip by contrast is more general purpose.
It's commonly used by photographers who want to quickly
stash a larger camera on their backpack while walking,
and its Arca Swiss compatibility opens the door
to more varied setups beyond just POV shooting.
So if you want to mount that doubles as part
of a bigger photography or videography kit,
the capture clip is likely more flexible.
Overall, both of these mounts are solid choices for over-the-shoulder POV footage.
The final results look very similar, with fairly minor differences in things like
how much of your head sneaks into the frame when you zoom out or pan around.
The magnetic holster shines if you want to go with a hybrid style of shooting,
switching seamlessly between backpack POV and handheld shots on a selfie stick.
It's the more convenient option if you're
constantly moving between these two shooting styles.
The capture clip on the other hand makes more sense if you want a dedicated
shoulder mounted POV camera that just stays in place,
or if you're already using another camera as your main
shooter and your 360 camera is more like a secondary camera.
It's lighter, less obtrusive and built to stay out of the way.
So in the end, it really comes down to your style of shooting,
hybrid flexibility favours the holster, while dedicated POVs favours the clip.

caption_lines.text: GoPro's adhesive mounts are arguably the most versatile option for mounting your GoPro to
most surfaces that more conventional mounts can't handle.
Follow these very simple steps for optimal attachment and your mount will be able to
stand up to the most extreme environments.
I'll be demonstrating the process on my brand new Smith Vantage helmet, but the same steps
apply to any surface you plan on attaching to.
You will need a few things; a flat or curved GoPro adhesive mount (depending on how flat
or curved your surface is), the GoPro quick release buckle and white rubber anti-vibration
locking plug, some isopropyl rubbing alcohol (available in any pharmacy or convenience
store), measuring tape and a pencil (for finding and marking the center line) and some sort
of clamping tool.
The first step, is to determine where you want to attach the adhesive mount.
The options on a helmet are endless, but some recommended points are front and center, top
center or on one of the sides.
I'm going to be mounting mine front and center, so I can capture forward-facing point of view
footage, as well as self portrait type footage.
At this point, you need to decide whether to use a flat or curved adhesive mount.
Taking into account the curve of the helmet - it looks like the curved one will work best
in this situation.
I want my GoPro to be perfectly centered to minimize adjustments in post production, so
I need to find a center line to follow.
To do this, find two symmetrical points that are equally spaced apart (in this case the
two front vents).
Measure the distance between the points, and make a mark exactly half way between them.
Always, make sure to double check your work to avoid a crooked mount.
Now that we have our first point, we need to make another one to get a straight line.
Find another two symmetrical points (in this case the two vents that are on top of the
helmet), and make another mark.
Now use the tape measure or other straight edge to connect the two lines - this is your
center line.
The GoPro adhesive mounts use 3M VHB adhesive tape, and 3M has a pretty long instruction
manual on proper surface preparation.
To put it simply, the surface must be completely clean and free of any dirts or oils.
For most applications, they recommend using a 50:50 mixture of isopropyl alcohol and water.
Mix these two together, apply it to some sort of cloth or towel and rub the surface to prep
it for adhesion.
You might rub off some of your center line in the process, but that's why I made it longer
than I needed.
Now grab your adhesive mount, peel off its backing and slowly apply it while aligning
its' center with your center line.
Once you are happy with its' placement, apply as much pressure as you can with your hands.
The strength of the bond takes up to 72 hours to reach 100% of its potential, and maintaining
pressure on it will aid that process.
So for optimal adhesion, you can use some c-clamps, spring clamps or some sort of other
clamp to sustain pressure on it for an extended period of time.
This step is not absolutely necessary, but I like to take all the precautions possible
when it comes to these pricey little cameras.
If this video helped you avoid a sticky situation with your adhesive GoPro mounts, give me a
thumbs up, share it with your friends and subscribe for more GoPro tips and DIYs!
